title: Cardiopulmonary bypass principles and cannulation techniques
subject: ss-ctvs
refs: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Extracorporeal Circulation and Cardiopulmonary Bypass)
STS/SCA Practice Guidelines on Cardiopulmonary Bypass

steps.say: Extracorporeal circulation temporarily takes over cardiopulmonary function during open heart procedures. Systemic deoxygenated blood drains into an artificial oxygenator through venous cannulas. A mechanical arterial pump reinfuses freshly oxygenated blood into the aorta under physiological pressure.
steps.tx: Cardiopulmonary bypass diverts deoxygenated venous return from the right atrium or venae cavae into an artificial **membrane oxygenator** for gas exchange. A calibrated mechanical pump continuously returns fully saturated blood into the **ascending aorta**, sustaining systemic arterial perfusion while the heart is arrested.

nodes.label: Venous drainage via right atrium or cavae
Cardiotomy reservoir and gas exchange in oxygenator
Mechanical pump generation of arterial head
Arterial reinfusion into distal ascending aorta

steps.say: Safe initiation of bypass requires robust systemic anticoagulation. Clinicians administer intravenous unfractionated heparin before cannulation to prevent catastrophic thrombotic occlusion across artificial surfaces. Surgical teams verify an activated clotting time exceeding four hundred and eighty seconds before running the pump.
steps.tx: Systemic anticoagulation requires **unfractionated heparin** administered at an initial loading dose of 300 to 400 units per kilogram. Surgeons confirm that the **activated clotting time** exceeds 480 seconds before opening venous lines, ensuring complete platelet and thrombin inhibition during extracorporeal contact.

steps.say: Once the cardiac repair finishes and the patient separates from bypass, heparin reversal restores hemostasis. The team slowly infuses protamine sulfate based on initial heparin units. Protamine binds negatively charged heparin molecules into an inert salt, returning clotting times to baseline.
steps.tx: Following decannulation from bypass, **protamine sulfate** rapidly neutralizes circulating heparin at a standard ratio of 1 to 1.3 mg per 100 units of administered heparin. The anesthesiologist titrates this slow infusion to return the **activated clotting time** to baseline while watching for pulmonary vasoconstriction.

left.title: Heparin Anticoagulation
points: Prevents clotting on plastic circuit tubing

right.title: Protamine Reversal
points: Dosed at 1 to 1.3 mg per 100 heparin units

steps.say: Specific clinical scenarios prevent conventional heparin administration. In patients with active heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, bivalirudin serves as a direct thrombin inhibitor during bypass. Patients who have true antithrombin deficiency require fresh frozen plasma or antithrombin concentrate to restore heparin sensitivity.
steps.tx: Patients diagnosed with **heparin-induced thrombocytopenia** require specialized non-heparin anticoagulation during urgent bypass procedures, making **bivalirudin** the preferred direct thrombin inhibitor. Conversely, individuals exhibiting severe heparin resistance due to inherited or acquired **antithrombin III deficiency** receive donor fresh frozen plasma or purified antithrombin concentrate before cannulation.

rows: Infusion of FFP or antithrombin concentrate
Fish hypersensitivity or NPH insulin exposure

steps.say: Arterial cannulation delivers oxygenated blood directly into the patient arterial tree. Surgeons insert the primary arterial cannula into the distal ascending aorta just proximal to the innominate takeoff. In cases of extensive aortic pathology, the right axillary or common femoral artery provides reliable peripheral inflow.
steps.tx: Primary **arterial cannulation** enters the distal **ascending aorta** immediately proximal to the innominate takeoff, avoiding atherosclerotic plaques and fragile calcified tissue. When ascending aortic dissection or extensive circumferential calcification precludes central access, surgical teams select peripheral cannulation through the right **axillary artery** or the common femoral vessel.

left.title: Central Aortic Cannulation
points: Avoids peripheral vascular injury or groin cutdown

right.title: Peripheral Cannulation
points: Axillary or femoral artery cannulation site
Essential for acute dissection and reoperations
Carries potential risks of retrograde malperfusion

steps.say: Venous drainage depends on the planned intracardiac exposure. Routine coronary bypass uses a single two-stage venous cannula positioned through the right atrial appendage into the inferior vena cava. Operations requiring open right heart chambers necessitate bicaval cannulation with snug caval tourniquets.
steps.tx: Coronary revascularization utilizes a **two-stage cannula** placed through the right atrium into the inferior vena cava. Conversely, procedures requiring right atrium or septum opening demand **bicaval cannulation** with **caval snaring** to prevent air aspiration and eliminate venous return into the operative field.

nodes.label: Coronary bypass without open chambers: two-stage cannula
Tricuspid or transseptal exposure: individual bicaval cannulae
Caval snaring to achieve bloodless intracardiac field

steps.say: Left heart decompression prevents dangerous cavity overdistention during aortic cross-clamping. Surgeons place a vent cannula into the left ventricle through the right superior pulmonary vein. Decompression protects the myocardium against elevated wall stress, subendocardial ischemia, and pulmonary capillary congestion.
steps.tx: Inserting a dedicated **left ventricular vent** through the **right superior pulmonary vein** provides continuous left heart cavity decompression. By actively venting bronchial collateral venous return and subtle aortic regurgitation, this maneuver eliminates ventricular distention, halts progressive **subendocardial ischemia**, and prevents retrograde pulmonary venous hypertension throughout the cross-clamp period.

nodes.label: Accumulation of bronchial and Thebesian venous return
Active aspiration via right superior pulmonary vein vent
Prevention of left ventricular wall stretch and ischemia

steps.say: Maintaining systemic hemodynamics preserves end-organ function while on cardiopulmonary bypass. Perfusionists target a cardiac index between two point two and two point four liters per minute per square meter under mild hypothermia. Mean arterial pressure is maintained between fifty and eighty millimeters of mercury.
steps.tx: Systemic perfusion during bypass maintains a target **cardiac index** of 2.2 to 2.4 L/min/m2 alongside a **mean arterial pressure** of 50 to 80 mmHg. This controlled flow rate guarantees adequate **systemic perfusion**, shielding cerebral, renal, and splanchnic microvascular beds from hypoperfusion injury.

rows: Guarantees adequate global tissue oxygen delivery
Preserves cerebral and renal autoregulatory thresholds
Confirms global balance of oxygen supply and uptake
